title: A Grip That Signals and Feels Force

scenes.visual: Carried world opens immediately in gentle motion: a dark-slate canvas showing an amber vessel wall (#D4A359) studded with gold ligand handles (#F5C542) along the bottom, a white blood cell drifting left-to-right in flowing blood at top. Title text 'A Grip That Signals and Feels Force' fades cleanly across the upper frame in crisp white (size 38) and clears at 2.0 s.

scenes.tts: A white blood cell racing in blood can stop on a vessel wall in about a second. Its gripping receptor has no enzyme, so how does it switch on fast and send signals inside?
scenes.caption: A white blood cell racing in blood can stop on a vessel wall in about a second. Its gripping receptor has no enzyme, so how does it switch on fast and send signals inside?
scenes.visual: The white blood cell slows and arrests on the amber vessel wall (#D4A359). Camera zooms smoothly into the underside of the cell to establish the single carried cross-section filling 65% of the frame height: amber matrix/wall at the bottom with gold handles (#F5C542), slate-blue plasma membrane (#5C7A99) across the middle, silver-white actin filaments (#E2E8F0) drifting gently in the cytoplasm above.
scenes.narration: A white blood cell racing in blood can stop on a vessel wall in about a second. Its gripping receptor has no enzyme, so how does it switch on fast and send signals inside?

scenes.tts: The receptor that grabs hold is an integrin. It is built from two different chains, alpha and beta, each crossing the membrane once. Outside, their large parts form a head that grips the matrix, the protein mesh cells sit on, or proteins on other cells. Inside, two short tails face actin, with no kinase and no channel.

scenes.visual: In the same membrane cross-section, one integrin highlights: a teal alpha chain (#2EC4B6) and a coral beta chain (#FF6B6B), each spanning the slate-blue bilayer once, shown as clean labelled geometric blocks (no atomic structures). Outer legs and a cleft head point toward the amber matrix (#D4A359) and gold RGD/ligand handles (#F5C542). Bold labels (size 28+): 'α chain', 'β chain', 'short tails', 'no enzyme'. Corner label: 'schematic'.

scenes.tts: A hormone receptor waits quietly until a soluble ligand arrives. Many integrins are bathed in ligand all the time. Think of a platelet floating through blood that is already rich in fibrinogen, its sticky partner. Why does that platelet not clump on the spot?
scenes.caption: A hormone receptor waits quietly until a soluble ligand arrives. Many integrins are bathed in ligand all the time. Think of a platelet floating through blood that is already rich in fibrinogen, its sticky partner. Why does that platelet not clump on the spot?
scenes.visual: Gold ligand bars labelled 'fibrinogen' (#F5C542) drift continuously past the teal-and-coral integrin in the slate-blue membrane. The integrin's outer legs fold at a visible knee so its head tips back toward the membrane, staying closed while ligands bump gently past without sticking. Question card fades in cleanly at top: 'Platelets float in fibrinogen. Why do they not clump right away?'
scenes.narration: A hormone receptor waits quietly until a soluble ligand arrives. Many integrins are bathed in ligand all the time. Think of a platelet floating through blood that is already rich in fibrinogen, its sticky partner. Why does that platelet not clump on the spot?

scenes.visual: Thinking pause: the question card stays readable at full contrast while gold fibrinogen bars continue drifting slowly past the bent, closed teal-and-coral integrin on the slate-blue membrane, with a subtle circular timer ring ticking across 4.5 seconds.

scenes.tts: Because the cell controls the receptor itself. In platelet and white blood cell integrins, the outer legs fold at a knee. Bent with the head closed, the grip stays weak. An inside signal recruits talin and kindlin to the beta tail, and the two tails separate. That change passes through the membrane, so the legs straighten and the head opens tight.
scenes.caption: Because the cell controls the receptor itself. In platelet and white blood cell integrins, the outer legs fold at a knee. Bent with the head closed, the grip stays weak. An inside signal recruits talin and kindlin to the β tail, and the two tails separate. That change passes through the membrane, so the legs straighten and the head opens tight.
scenes.visual: Question clears. A violet block labelled 'talin' (#9B72CF) and a smaller violet-slate partner labelled 'kindlin' glide down from the cytoplasm and dock on the coral beta tail (#FF6B6B). The teal and coral tails and transmembrane helices visibly pry apart. That motion propagates down the outer legs: the knee straightens smoothly, the head cleft opens wide, and it snaps tightly onto a gold handle (#F5C542) on the amber matrix.
scenes.narration: Because the cell controls the receptor itself. In platelet and white blood cell integrins, the outer legs fold at a knee. Bent with the head closed, the grip stays weak. An inside signal recruits talin and kindlin to the β tail, and the two tails separate. That change passes through the membrane, so the legs straighten and the head opens tight.

scenes.tts: Nothing new had to be made, so a platelet or white blood cell can grab hold fast. Because the message starts in the cytoplasm and changes grip outside, this is inside-out signalling. Once bound integrins cluster on a solid surface, the message reverses and runs inward.
scenes.caption: Nothing new had to be made, so a platelet or white blood cell can grab hold fast. Because the message starts in the cytoplasm and changes grip outside, this is inside-out signalling. Once bound integrins cluster on a solid surface, the message reverses and runs inward.
scenes.visual: A bright downward arrow labelled 'inside-out' sweeps from the cytoplasm through the extended integrin to the locked matrix handle. Then two neighbouring bent integrins straighten and slide laterally along the slate-blue membrane to cluster beside the first one on the amber matrix, reversing the arrow upward into the cell ('outside-in').
scenes.narration: Nothing new had to be made, so a platelet or white blood cell can grab hold fast. Because the message starts in the cytoplasm and changes grip outside, this is inside-out signalling. Once bound integrins cluster on a solid surface, the message reverses and runs inward.

scenes.tts: Clustered integrins assemble a focal adhesion on their short tails. Talin links the beta tail to actin, and paxillin forms a docking scaffold. With no enzyme of its own, the cluster borrows focal adhesion kinase. Folded shut at rest, it opens and phosphorylates one of its own tyrosines. That phosphate docks Src, another kinase, and the pair phosphorylates neighbours.
scenes.caption: Clustered integrins assemble a focal adhesion on their short tails. Talin links the β tail to actin, and paxillin forms a docking scaffold. scenes.visual: On the clustered coral beta tails (#FF6B6B), violet talin rods (#9B72CF) bridge up to silver-white actin filaments (#E2E8F0) while a scaffold bar labelled 'paxillin' docks beside them. A cyan hinged block labelled 'FAK' (#38BDF8) enters folded shut (FERM cap covering kinase), swings open at the cluster, flashes a bright yellow phosphate starburst (#FACC15, labelled 'Tyr397'), and then the yellow phosphate docks a cyan partner labelled 'Src' that stamps yellow phosphates onto FAK and paxillin. Corner note: 'schematic'.

scenes.tts: The same adhesion also feels how hard it is being pulled. The motor protein myosin drags actin inward against the anchored matrix. Talin's rod hides binding sites for vinculin, a linker that also grips actin. Tension stretches the rod and uncovers those buried sites. Vinculin then clips talin to actin, strengthening the grip without adding any phosphate.

scenes.visual: A crimson bar labelled 'myosin' (#F87171) pulls the silver-white actin filament leftward while the amber matrix below holds firm. A compact force gauge beside the violet talin rod rises (marked 'tension, schematic'). The violet rod elongates as folded segments open to reveal glowing yellow pockets (#FFE066). Magenta clips labelled 'vinculin' (#E85D9E) snap into the exposed pockets and grab the actin filament, visibly thickening the mechanical bridge.

scenes.tts: Integrin grip switches from inside, and focal adhesions signal and sense force. Inside cues straighten a bent receptor into a firm hold. Once bound and pulled, the complex borrows kinases and adds extra links under load. Whether other adhesion proteins unfold the same way stays open. Next, actin switches turn grip into movement.

scenes.visual: Camera pulls slightly back on the same live cross-section so all three mechanisms pulse gently in sequence: violet talin holding the teal/coral integrin extended on amber matrix (inside-out), cyan FAK-Src glowing with yellow phosphates on paxillin (outside-in), and stretched talin with magenta vinculin clips holding taut silver-white actin (force sensing). Clean visual clear before end card.

scenes.visual: End card on deep-slate background, high contrast, single line only with no smaller line underneath: 'Integrin grip switches from inside, and focal adhesions signal and sense force.'
